i am in favour of the compromise reached on the proposal for a directive because, despite some problems, i think it is a good text which protects the patient from the great dangers of taking falsified medicines. over the years we have seen a huge increase in the number of counterfeit medicines, and the latest estimates put the number of illegal drugs sold in europe at about one and a half million, mainly via the internet. these data pose a serious threat not only to patients but also to european manufacturers. the protection of public health is at stake, as is the protection of consumers, who must be guaranteed strict safety measures and effective penalties by the member states. today's vote will introduce effective and flexible rules and will also deal with the fight against organised crime. to appreciate the need for security in the industry, consider that some 34 million illegal drugs were seized in 2008. perhaps a little more courage would have been needed in the matter of the traceability of medicines and active ingredients from third countries: but the one we have achieved today is still an important milestone.
mr president, the commission's proposal on preventing the entry of falsified medicines into the pharmaceutical chain highlights a concern which is becoming a priority for all european citizens: the quality and safety of the medicines we use every day. a new european strategy is therefore needed to combat the widespread spread of falsified medicines, with the dual aim of responding to this growing threat to public health and ensuring the safety of all patients. the latest reports on this subject have in fact recorded a real surge in the seizure of counterfeit medicines at customs, as well as an ever-increasing and therefore very dangerous tendency to counterfeit not only so-called comfort medicines but also life-saving medicines, including medicines for the treatment of cancer, heart disease, psychiatric disorders and infections.
mr president, the increase in the number of counterfeit medicines seized at the eu's borders in 2007 was 384 per cent compared with 2005. we have also seen an increase in the tendency to counterfeit even life-saving medicines, including medicines for cancer and heart disease, psychiatric disorders and infections. these data describe an alarming scenario in which patients risk facing situations such as treatment failure, endangering their health and, in some cases, their lives. i welcome the commission's proposal. however, the report by mrs matias correctly highlights the negative aspects and the points on which we cannot refrain from giving our citizens assurances. in particular, i would like to emphasize that the commission proposal does not provide exhaustive answers on the nature and characteristics of a falsified medicinal product, an active ingredient or an excipient, nor on the definitions concerning the various actors in the pharmaceutical chain, whose roles and responsibilities must be clarified. the penalties in the commission proposal are not adequate, but above all it does not take account of the sale of medicines on the internet, one of the main channels for counterfeit medicines to enter the european market.
mr president, i voted in favour of mrs matias's text because the introduction of falsified medicines into legal supply chains is a threat to the whole european pharmaceutical system, because it undermines the confidence that citizens have in the quality of medicines sold in pharmacies and other places of legal distribution. it is important to put a stop to the gradual increase in the number of falsified medicines in all european countries, in order to protect and guarantee the health of our citizens. the active ingredients in a falsified medicinal product may be of lower quality than the standard, may be completely absent, or may be in the wrong dosage.
mr president, the official figures are clear: 1% of medicines legally sold in the european union are counterfeit. as if that were not enough, the latest investigations show that the phenomenon is steadily increasing and its proportions have now passed the guard level. as mr antoniozzi has already pointed out, the counterfeiting of life-saving medicines is particularly profitable when the production takes place in india or china and is then sold as european production. the dangers of these substances are unprecedented and can endanger the lives of those who use them for therapeutic purposes. i voted in favour of the report to say no to the wild west of online sales, the preferential entry channel that allows these poisons to enter the eu pharmaceutical market illegally. the adoption of this document will enable parliament to finally make its voice heard and to have the necessary instruments to find and punish these real dealers, these unscrupulous criminals who have been making their fortunes on the backs of sick people for too long.
mr president, the problem of falsified medicines is one which is having an increasingly widespread impact at international and community level, both because of the increase in the number of cases and because of the increase in the degree of sophistication of the cases. it is to these challenges that mr matias' report - the result of long and laborious negotiations - seeks to respond. this report, which we supported, defined a regulatory framework which, starting from more precise and detailed definitions, took into account all the actors, the moments and the dimensions of the pharmaceutical chain - safety, traceability, obligations for the distribution chain - and achieved a good compromise. these are some of the areas where we must try to work to achieve the main objective of establishing stricter standards, to prevent the entry of falsified medicines, and to achieve a positive and more complete regulatory framework capable of safeguarding the health of citizens, protecting them from the risk of serious consequences.
mr president, i voted in favour of the resolution on the progress of croatia's accession to the european union in the context of the enlargement process, because i consider both the start of this process and the progress made by croatia to be very important. what we want is basically that enlargement should not only extend to croatia but also to the whole of the western balkans. this is one of the central points of both the neighbourhood and enlargement policies of europe. i therefore express my strong support for the swoboda report.
mr president, the resolution adopted today sets out important principles for consumer protection, by increasing the safeguards against the spread of falsified medicines. this is a very dangerous phenomenon and one of the most significant remedies is to stop the sale of questionable medicines online and through the adoption of a series of safeguards we will have a strict regulation that requires authorization and controls. however, this does not mean that the forms of health protection and medical prescriptions are being cancelled out. it should be recalled that this does not affect the legislative power of the member states in this area and that they may maintain or restrict the prohibition on the sale of medicinal products online in their territory. this is an opportunity for the member states to regulate the matter better, but it must be remembered, mr president, that citizens can order medicines from another member state and that the opportunity for regulation must not be another opportunity to privilege the caste of pharmacists, but we must continue along this path of liberalization that the european union is charting with measures like this.
mr president, the number of counterfeit medicines has increased exponentially in recent years and it is regrettable that, despite a 384% increase in sales of these medicines from 2005 to 2007, the commission has been so late in coming up with an initiative. we are absolutely convinced of the positions of the rapporteur, who has tried to improve the commission's text, also dealing with the sale of medicines via the internet. i have asked the commission several times over the years about this matter and have warned of the danger, but i have never received any answers or any concrete initiative. we therefore welcome the rapporteur's efforts to improve the text today, and hope that the health of citizens will henceforth be a real priority for our institutions.
mr president, i voted in favour of mrs matias' report because it is very important to raise safety standards and to establish effective, efficient and strict rules to prevent counterfeit medicines from being introduced into the european union. it is a requirement and a duty we have towards all european citizens, who are often unaware of the fact that they are buying a counterfeit medicine. i agree with the report's structure, which introduces obligations not only for distributors but also for all those involved in the supply chain. it is often in the various stages of the supply chain that risky products are introduced. the controls must not only be carried out at the time of marketing, but also at the sites where medicinal products and active ingredients are produced, including in third countries. but i have a question which they cannot help but express: i would have preferred the regulation to have regulated it more effectively, by harmonizing the different national laws, including online sales, to protect the european consumer 100 per cent.
mr president, i voted in favour of this report because the resulting regulatory framework is certainly better than the 2001 directive. the latter imposed obligations on wholesale distributors only, and did not guarantee the reliability of the pharmaceutical chain. the report voted today introduces measures which will further guarantee the safety of pharmaceutical products, such as intensified inspections of manufacturers outside the european union on the basis of risk analyses. the amendment also provides for the need to publish in a european database the list of certified wholesale distributors, i.e. who have not been found to comply with eu legislation by an inspection by the member state. however, a more ambitious result could be hoped for, especially by introducing mandatory inspections at the production sites of active ingredients in third countries. the latter were omitted on the grounds that the costs of implementation would be too high. if they had been introduced, it would have been possible to avoid once again that, while european companies have to meet very high quality standards, those producing in other regions of the world benefit from regulatory frameworks that are certainly less stringent. i hope that in future improvements will be made.
mr president, there are more than 100 million workers in europe today who depend directly or indirectly on small and mediumsized enterprises. yet small and mediumsized enterprises are facing an unprecedented crisis: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. so this is the meaning of this resolution: parliament called for guarantee programmes for loans and credits for small and medium-sized enterprises and for a vigorous european initiative to counterbalance the new - and for many enterprises prohibitive - bank requirements, particularly in respect of collateral guarantees and higher risk premiums. finally, i share the need to significantly increase funding under the competitiveness and innovation programme and to give a strong and determined boost to the theme of simplification: the commission has also proposed that the rules on the use of the funds be simplified and streamlined so that firms wishing to access the funds can do so without having to resort to costly external advice. i therefore voted in favour of this resolution: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect.
mr president, it is necessary to evaluate and review the existing instruments to support the financing of small and mediumsized enterprises in view of the forthcoming multiannual financial framework if we are to focus, also in this sector, on stimulating the recovery of the real economy with a view to finally overcoming the crisis. this is also necessary to protect the interests of small and medium-sized enterprises when setting higher capital requirements for banks as proposed by basel iii in terms of equity capital; is required by the situation of many financial intermediaries, discouraged by the administrative burdens created by complex european financial regulations; is influenced by the difficulties created by the different tax and support regimes and is suggested by the need to make the union support programmes coherent, in order to provide greater guarantees and a good balance between the national and union schemes. i therefore support the proposal to set up a single window for the various financing instruments for smes. simplifying offers and market access procedures is an important support even if more funding is needed. huge sums have been spent to save banks from sudden collapse: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has already taken a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos.
mr president, i voted in favour of the resolution because i am convinced that a european strategy is needed with regard to smes, which, as we all know, are the building blocks of our economy and must be supported and helped. the next financial programming of the european union cannot therefore ignore these considerations and must increase and diversify the resources available. but this is only one measure, and it is still not enough, and more must be added. it is important to act with the help of a long-term strategy, avoiding one-off or one-off buffer measures - i am referring to the new financial rules that the european union is about to put in place. these new regulations must not lead to a restriction of the granting of credit to firms - i am also referring to basle iii. this is the real new challenge: to reconcile and regulate the banking system, avoiding that the costs are passed on to firms, citizens and smes. it is growth that contributes to both the recovery and the support of the sector, moving from theoretical approaches to practice.
mr president, the demographic developments of recent years make it necessary to consider the need to implement a strategy capable of strengthening cohesion and consistency in the field of pensions, of promoting solidarity between generations and between individuals, while at the same time helping to guarantee a secure and adequate income after retirement. i agree with the rapporteur when she points out that there are great differences between pension systems in europe, which have been severely affected by the severe economic and financial crisis with the increase in unemployment, the fall in growth, the reduction in investment returns and the growth in public debt. pension funds have greater difficulty in securing adequate pensions and, in some cases, in honouring contractual commitments. many member states have made major cuts in their pension systems. financial sustainability is important, but the need to ensure adequate income must also be taken into account. sustainable budgets and adequate pension systems are not conflicting objectives but two sides of the same coin: true sustainability cannot be achieved without adequate retirement income. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations, and that it should be involved in the negotiations.
mr president, the efficiency of social spending, given the pressure it exerts on budgets, is now of fundamental importance in the economic systems of the member states. we have seen this in recent years, when we have seen an increase in unemployment, poverty and social exclusion, with the result that budget deficits in many member states have worsened, followed by problems in financing pensions. i welcome the report by mrs oomen-ruijten, which aims to give new impetus at national and european union level by contributing to the creation of sound, long-term adequate, sustainable and secure pension systems. i would like to take this opportunity to remind you that we do not yet have common criteria or definitions, nor a thorough analysis to explain the various pension systems in all their aspects and their adequacy in relation to the needs of citizens. i wonder how it is possible to tackle such a sensitive subject in the absence of such a study. i therefore call on the commission to remedy this shortcoming by taking appropriate action to classify the pension systems of the member states by type and to produce a set of common definitions which will make the systems compatible.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, in this unique and solemn moment, i recall the early days of the european convention when we were discussing how what used to be called the ‘democratic deficit of the european integration process’ could be eliminated, or at least reduced. there was a common goal which we all shared, and that was to enhance the democratic functioning of the european union. one way of doing that has just been found, and that is to foster the participation of the citizens themselves in the democratic life of the union. that is how, and that is why, the right of the citizens’ initiative was included in the treaty, and now citizens can approach the european commission directly and invite it to submit a proposal for a legislative act of the european union. i firmly believe that this is a milestone on the path towards more democracy in the union. it is also the first element of direct democracy. it establishes direct contact and dialogue between the institutions and citizens and encourages cross-border direct dialogue and cooperation. it also encourages a sense of ownership: europe is not them – europe is us, and europe will develop as we shape it ourselves, all of us together. yes, our motto, ‘a strong europe with a human touch’ depends upon all of us. to achieve these goals and to implement the treaty, clear, simple and user-friendly rules of procedure had to be established. this has now been done and was the result of the good cooperation between all the institutions – the commission, the council and first and foremost, the european parliament. i would like to extend my special thanks to mr maroš šefčovič of the commission; madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i fully share the concern about the rise in food prices and it could not be otherwise, since this is a problem which affects the lives of european citizens very closely and especially the less well-off classes. these increases make it impossible for the population of all developing countries to meet their basic food needs. the developed countries, including europe, cannot remain indifferent to this scenario. the new common agricultural policy must therefore include instruments to reduce price volatility, to limit speculation on agricultural commodities and to ensure an adequate level of production within the community. i must therefore stress that we cannot leave land unused at a time when the world population is increasing, and therefore the food supply must also increase.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i am pleased to inform you that, when the plane was touching down this morning in strasbourg, i got the good news that the hungarian prime minister has agreed to amend the media law so that it complies with all aspects of eu law that we, the european commission have raised, including the concerns raised regarding the charter of fundamental rights. they assure me that the amendments will be adopted by the hungarian government at its next session. the body language of the representatives of the hungarian government gives me the feeling that this is correct and that it will be tabled in the hungarian parliament within the coming days. the four areas where the hungarian authorities agreed to amend their law are the following. number one: balanced coverage. the amendments agreed would limit the balanced reporting requirements to broadcasting, as in other member states, and would no longer apply those requirements to on-demand audiovisual media services or the written press. moreover, any restrictions on broadcasters would need to respect the principle of proportionality. of course the commission will monitor the way that principle is translated into secondary law. i mentioned four areas. the second one is the country-of-origin principle. the amendments agreed would mean that foreign broadcasters could no longer be fined for breaching the hungarian media law’s provisions on protection of minors or incitement to hatred. instead the hungarian authorities could suspend transmission of such services on hungarian territory, which is in line with the avms directive. what does that mean? it means that broadcasters legally established and authorised in other member states, and compliant with the laws of those countries, would be free to broadcast to hungary without running the risk of being subject to fines by hungarian authorities.number three: media registration. the amendments agreed would mean that audiovisual media service providers would have to register only after they begin offering their services, and that is in line with the directive. it means that audiovisual media service providers and publishers would no longer be subject to prior authorisation by the hungarian authorities. number four: offensive content. additionally, the hungarian government agreed to amend another provision of its media law that raised concerns with respect to the freedom of expression. a provision of the media law specified very broadly that media content may not cause offence, even by implication, to individuals, minorities or majorities. the amendments agreed would limit the prohibition to discriminatory treatment. moreover those provisions would no longer apply to media service providers established in other eu countries. we will work closely with the hungarian authorities to make sure that the agreed changes are now adopted into hungarian law and applied in practice. we will continue to monitor the situation, but that is quite clear. needless to say, the commission is also verifying the national rules implementing the avms directive in other member states and will raise similar concerns where necessary. the commission does not shy away from using its powers. it does not shy away from defending media freedom and pluralism when it is needed, and the present case hopefully pre-empts and proves that. i can assure you that the commission acknowledges and shares the concerns that many of you and parts of civil society have about the general state of the media in europe. i am ready to go further and take action in the matter of media pluralism within the eu competences, of course respecting subsidiarity. the commission not only has a duty, but also a sincere interest, in facilitating the dialogue amongst stakeholders and policymakers at a european level. the changing structure of the media landscape in europe causes concern for the future. it brings opportunities but also wider risks for media pluralism beyond the ownership use. it is quite clear that we need an approach to measuring media pluralism in a broad sense; one that will bring together legal, economic and social aspects, rather than treating them quite separately, as has often been the case up until now. therefore, i intend to establish a multi-stakeholder group and ask them to address the challenges for the media at present and in the future, including the situation of media pluralism in europe. since you know that i value your input very much, the european parliament will be represented in the group of experts, if you will accept that invitation. i will announce details quite soon. the group will be asked to advise me on the next steps to be taken concerning the media landscape and i am fully committed to taking concrete action within all the competences that i have.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the hungarian government has shown a great deal of sensitivity to europe and to the principles on which it is based. in fact, immediately after the passing of the hungarian media law, there was a campaign unleashed by the left using the formula "mouth-watering law". in reality, only those who have experienced communism, fascism and nazism know what a gag law is, while democratic states know that freedom and pluralism of information are constitutive of democracy: but they must be in harmony with all the other powers of the rule of law and must not undermine, in particular, the foundation of democracy, which is human dignity. for example, the italian constitution itself, in article 21, guarantees freedom of information, but also directly prohibits publications contrary to good morals. the 1948 law on freedom of the press in italy, which no one has ever challenged, establishes the obligation not to grant permission but to register every publication, as does hungarian law. the reservations which the european commission has rightly expressed do not detract from the declared finality of the hungarian law, and this finality of respect for human dignity is demonstrated precisely by the attitude which the hungarian government has taken, by being readily open to accepting criticism and taking responsibility for changing the law according to the indications given to it. the statement that the fundamental rights of the european union will be enshrined in the hungarian constitution is also proof of this fundamental will of hungary to integrate into european culture. in conclusion, the only point of this debate is to blame hungary for having supported the government and parliament democratically by a two-thirds majority. but this is a cause for hope for europe, not for criticism. so i thank the commission for its work and i thank the hungarian government.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, a couple of the honourable members asked an intriguing question: is it a coincidence that today’s debate should coincide with the hungarian government’s decision? well, sometimes, mr president, you need a small angel at your shoulder. for my own part, i prefer, when you invite me to come, to make clear what is at stake, to be able to come armed with facts and figures. is what has happened today a coincidence? the answer i will give to that comes, in a way, straight from my heart. we are talking about an entire procedure: it started at the end of december and we are now half way through february – so it has taken a bit more than seven weeks. well, in the light of the six years i have been in office in the european institutions, that is quite speedy. my experience so far has been that things are rarely so speedy that i feel we can solve a problem within seven weeks. having said that, the background to today’s outcome is fascinating. we have a combination of factors. firstly, we are not talking about this issue for the first time. you have invited me to discuss it before. you have been quite clear, so there has been no doubt about what is at stake – no doubt about what every party in this house thinks on this question. secondly, we are talking about a very important issue. i do not need to explain to you that the issue of freedom of expression and freedom of the press is what is at stake for the commission; and that it would be ridiculous if we did not make that a top priority with regard to defending democracy. was it a coincidence that the previous item on the agenda this afternoon was the situation in egypt? you have been talking about creating democracy, so there is a clear thread here, and you can be absolutely certain that the commission is aware of that and is, indeed, doing its utmost to defend democracy and to repair it where it may have been attacked. the third issue is, of course, the hungarian presidency. let us not be naive. of course our friends in this member state within the family of europe are aware that, for those in the chair, noblesse oblige. so from their side too there has been an approach of doing their utmost to solve the problem. the final point i would make in this explanation, in so far as i can offer one, is that the european parliament has been crystal clear: you have been fighting and you have been keeping the outside world informed via the press – via a free press, i would add. so do not underestimate your own role. having said that, for me the whole combination of factors is, at the end of the day, the explanation of why we have this result at this point of time. fundamental rights are the issue that has been at stake: there is no doubt about that. anyone who thinks that i am interested only in peace and quiet does not know me in the least, because i am fighting for democracy. i do have a fair bit of experience and i have had a longer life in politics than most of you. let me touch, also, on a couple of the specific issues about which i was asked. what about the independence of the media regulator? our preliminary analysis of the hungarian law concludes that the procedures for nominating and electing the president and members of the media council are no different from those that are commonly accepted in europe. we have to acknowledge – whether it furthers our case or not – that the governing party holds a two-thirds majority, and that, in a democracy, is a simple fact. (applause) on the question of the application of article 11 of the charter of fundamental rights, we are applying the directive – the avms directive – and the treaty, and that implies of course applying article 11 of the charter. so there is no doubt about that. mr moraes said there was no judicial review of decisions by the media authority. a decision by the media council, passed in its capacity as an authority of the first instance, cannot be appealed via an administrative procedure. however, as provided for in article 163, an official decision of the media council may be challenged in court in accordance with the provisions of the code of civil procedure. the lodging of the appeal does not have suspensory effect but the code may be invoked to suspend the execution of the decision. ms weber said that the protection of sources under the hungarian media law is insufficient. if we take press freedom as a basic european principle, that should be the starting point and the ultimate end in all our thinking on this subject. i have always defended press freedom at european level and i will continue – and i promise you the commission will continue – to promote it untiringly. the right of journalists to protect their sources is one of the main principles guaranteeing the effective exercise of press freedom. journalists should never be required to reveal their sources unless it is necessary for them to do so for the purposes of a criminal investigation, and that principle is valid whatever the political climate. in fact, it needs to be defended with more passion whenever the press and the media generally are in a weaker position, as is the case nowadays. the directive on privacy and electronic communications currently in force requires the member states to ensure the confidentiality of communications. however, the directive does not apply to activities which fall outside the scope of the eu treaties. that is to say that eu law does not apply to matters relating to public security, defence, state security or the enforcement of criminal law and, moreover, under the principle of subsidiarity, member states have the possibility of taking measures that could restrict an individual’s right to privacy, in accordance with their own rules and with the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. any such restriction must be necessary, appropriate and proportionate within a democratic society, and a commissioner is not in a position to judge or condemn such national doings, nor do i wish to do so. on the matter of the absence of reference to article 30 – and a number of members have asked about that – i know that many of you have complained that the commission has not taken article 30 fully into account when assessing the media law. i should like to say loudly and clearly: that is simply not true. although in its original proposal for the avms directive the commission had included an obligation on the member states to guarantee the independence of the national regulatory authorities – and i know full well that your memory on such matters is excellent – that provision was not supported by the council and, despite strong support from the european parliament, it was changed into the current article 30 of the avms directive. the final wording of the avms directive does not directly establish an obligation to create independent bodies. it is not what we would have wished but it is what was written down in the text and we have to accept it, albeit with regret. the hungarian authorities have agreed to delete the provision in question and add the following declaratory text to article 10 of the media constitution, and i quote: ‘it is the task for the entirety of the media system to provide authentic, rapid and accurate information on such affairs and events’. so that will be the text after the changes. i have to apologise that you did not receive the text, but i myself did not receive it or, at least, i had only the text that we were negotiating and i could not distribute that to you. however, as soon as it is possible, i will supply you with the text. of course – while i hope you believe what i am saying and i would appreciate that – i imagine that, at the end of the day, you want to see it in writing and have the opportunity to read it. one of the issues that will make sense for you when you are making up your minds is that of the balanced reporting requirements: as i said in my opening remarks, these will no longer apply to the written press or to on-demand audiovisual media services. on the question, which mr løkkegaard asked, of whether i am ready to propose legislation on media pluralism, i said in my opening remarks that i am ready to take action in the matter of media pluralism within the existing eu competences. there is no one-size-fits-all approach: that is clear to me, and the hungarian case has made it even clearer. i will set up the working group to which i referred, and i thank you for your willingness to join it, in order to discuss the challenges we are facing, to make sure we have a comprehensive overview of the situation in europe and, of course, to act accordingly – including on the question of media independence. that should be one of the main priorities. with regard to the position of the osce on the hungarian media legislation, in relation to our own analysis, there is a difference of legal bases, but the osce was quite clear and quite right in its conclusions. the main issues raised by the osce concern the new media authority, in particular the long duration of the term of office of its members and the regulation of the public service broadcaster. i have explained the commission’s point of view here, and i think that the terms of office of members of other broadcasting councils, for example in other member states, range in some cases from five to nine years. one example but it is not the only one, is the rundfunkräte (public broadcasting boards). the crucial thing – and this is my final remark – is the message from the deputy prime minister that i received this morning when i touched down, and i am certain that the minister of foreign affairs will repeat the message that the hungarian government wrote down for me, and for the commission, stating what the position is. during the seven weeks in which we closely cooperated, i had already been impressed by the input of my own staff who had been working like hell. but i can assure you that both sides worked like hell and that they did their jobs not just in the proper way but in a constructive way, in order to find a solution, because this is a very important matter, and we have to find a solution.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would not like what we are discussing at this very moment to be another, perhaps final, fatal blow to the economy of our territories. we are already being invaded by low-cost or very low-cost goods, mainly from east and southeast asia. many italian enterprises, especially small and mediumsized ones, are suffering because of unfair competition, which does not allow them to compete on the market, with tragic consequences from the economic and above all employment point of view. this agreement provides for safeguard clauses and various protections: but who is to say that these rules are actually enforced? there are still too many unknowns and the possible advantage for a few large producers cannot always fall on the smaller ones. in my region, tuscany, there is a textile sector - historically a major textile industry - which is already in serious trouble because of asian competition: i would not like europe itself to be the one to give the final blow to this sector, as it probably will to many others, with this agreement. we're not voting for this deal.
the free trade agreement with the republic of korea is described by all as the institutional and strategic innovation of the union. it is an unbalanced agreement which will have a negative effect on european manufacturing. the zeroing of tariffs on korean products against the raising of environmental and social standards in korea cannot be considered fair. the korean shipbuilding industry has benefited from substantial state aid, which has enabled it to hold 30 percent of the world market. the european industry, whether it be the automobile, textile, chemical or other industries, will have to defend itself against competition which, if it is not unfair in form, is unfair in fact. the introduction of the safeguard clause is an appropriate measure but not sufficient to deal with the many weaknesses of the agreement. i therefore call on the european commission to be more cautious if it really wants to defend europe's economic interests.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in our daily work in parliament we realise that the added value is provided by access to selected information which supports our legislative and policy work. we use external human resources, which provide analysis and insight into the political, social, industrial and business realities. however, politics is made up of decisions and choices, and those remain entirely the responsibility of the politicians. it is about making choices that can be supported by groups of experts with high professional standards, specific levels of competence and able to express their opinions in a balanced way. hence the need to identify effective instruments and transparent procedures which enable the commission to carry out its role with the support of these groups of independent or autonomous experts. we know that this is a very problematic area. the 2010 plan is certainly a significant step forward, but much more needs to be done. the quality and authority of the experts also depend on the degree of their autonomy and the degree of their ability to support political decisions with fairness and loyalty. in the commission as in parliament, however, the mechanisms for publicity, the web and other effective means can be further simplified. so the right of access is good, the right of transparency is good, the right of balance between the right of transparency and what cannot be entrusted and handed over and made recognizable is good. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. but we must once again insist on the primacy of politics. if the policy is credible and competent, the role of the experts is one of advice and support. the decision is in any case up to the one who takes responsibility for it.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to point out that last week six important member states of the european union - france, germany, italy, spain, poland and portugal - said that europe must be less naive. the six countries call for a more effective and strategic defence of european external trade, since the existence and development of the european economic and social model are at stake. the six countries point out that the european union has opened up 80 per cent of its market to third countries, while the other major developed economies have only opened up 20 per cent. it is therefore argued that there are asymmetries in foreign trade and that the concept of reciprocity needs to be developed. this has brought many of our small and mediumsized enterprises to their knees, because they are subject to unfair competition which does not allow them to be competitive in the markets. mr president, i come from prato, a town which was once considered one of the most important textile districts in europe. today, because of unfair asian competition, it has become a ghost town, because the work of the prato entrepreneur has been distorted. for all these reasons, we have voted against this agreement.
i voted against the report, mr president, because i find it unacceptable that investment in third countries should be supported instead of being facilitated for the benefit of european small and mediumsized enterprises, which are the most important economic fabric of the union. i am firmly against the inclusion of turkey among the pre-accession candidate countries: i would remind you that turkey is still illegally occupying part of the territory of cyprus, which is a member state of the european union. in addition, there is no guarantee of transparency in the granting of community loans and grants by the eib to third countries. i would remind you that the resources of the eib are contributed by the citizens of europe and that is why priority should be given to investments within europe itself. many of the projects supported by the eib are located in countries where there is fighting and rebellion against various regimes. the report also envisages extending the community guarantees to other countries, such as cuba, which are notoriously lacking in democracy.
mr president, while we voted in favour of the safeguard clause in mr zalba's report, and i thank him again for his excellent work, we regrettably abstained on the trade agreement with korea. we regretfully did so because, while it is true that this agreement opens up a new, important market for the union, paving the way for future new trade agreements with other economic partners of the union, it is also true that many doubts and perplexities remain. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. in a europe where the rules for the designation of origin of products outside the european union have not yet been defined, we continue to offer privileged import positions for products on european territory, without requiring rules of true equality for businesses and knowledge for the citizens who buy. our abstention confirms that we are in favour of a free market with the necessary guarantees, while we are against the conclusion of trade agreements which do not sufficiently guarantee the rules of competition.

in writing. - i supported this text because i believe that the bilateral safeguard clause of the eu-korea free trade agreement is an effective instrument for defending european products. the entry into force of this agreement next july is expected to create difficulties for the european internal market. the gradual elimination of customs barriers on a bilateral basis will cause a significant increase in imports from korea. i am pleased to note that it will be possible to introduce specific measures even when the increase in imports into europe is concentrated in certain areas only. this measure is in line with italy's request for the introduction of a genuine 'regional safeguard clause', applicable only to certain regions of the eu. closing ourselves off from the international market is not only impossible but also harmful. but this presupposes that any opening up must be balanced and progressive, and that it takes account of the internal needs of the european union. the protection of jobs remains a priority for europe, as does the quality of the products that are marketed, and only by respecting these fundamental parameters will it be possible to build fruitful economic relations for both sides.
in writing. − we are in favour of the bilateral safeguard clause in the eu-korea free trade agreement because it mitigates the harmful effects of the measure. the purpose of this clause is to allow the suspension or re-application of duties if it is found that trade liberalization has caused serious damage to our industrial system. the safeguard clause will only be applicable for a maximum period of 10 years after the customs duties have been abolished. it is clear that the introduction of this clause does not change our position in voting against the text of the free trade agreement, which is still causing serious economic damage to our companies.
in writing. − the european union provides the european investment bank with a budgetary guarantee to cover the political and sovereign risks associated with its lending and guaranteeing activities in support of projects outside the european union. this community guarantee is an effective means of combining the budgetary resources of the union and the eib's own resources, while ensuring that the financial soundness of the eib is not compromised. the eib has already made considerable progress in implementing its mandate: strengthened coordination with the commission and focused its attention on supporting the union's policy objectives. the development of its external action will now have to translate into an increase in the volume of loans, their quality and the diversification of new beneficiaries (local authorities). an additional mandate of eur 500 million dedicated to microcredit financing should be granted without delay to increase access to bank financing for the most disadvantaged in eligible countries. in terms of internal organisation, the eib should be progressively encouraged to allocate all its external activities on a geographical basis in order to better adapt to the specific features of each area and to encourage the participation of partner countries.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in these years of recovery from the economic and financial crisis which has hit many of the countries of the union, in which our governments are working to implement common policies and strategies to achieve the objectives which we have all identified and decided to pursue together, i believe it is important to recognise the right and proper centrality of parliament as the most representative institution of the european union. it is a question of recognizing its representativeness and its function also in relation to what is enshrined in the treaties. the importance of the guidelines for economic and employment policies must certainly be at the heart of the european semester, and they must be adapted to changes in the annual assessment of growth and to the timing of implementation in our countries. the advisory function deserves the right space and the right time for analysis and adaptation to the overall framework. i therefore vote in favour.
in writing. - i would like to express my concern about the current situation in the world of work. i believe that unemployment is the real social problem of our time. despite the good signs of recovery at the macroeconomic level, industry will not be able to absorb all the workers it has laid off in recent months and who are facing difficulties in reintegrating into the market, as well as young people and women. these are matters of the utmost importance and urgency. in the 2020 strategy, the commission identified the promotion of employment, the strengthening of the single market and the encouragement of growth as priority objectives. the european union and this parliament in particular have done well in addressing this problem, but concrete action is needed to achieve these goals. the european union must work to channel and rationalise its resources by investing in transport, energy and telecommunications infrastructure: the breakthrough in this regard will be the creation of project companies guaranteed and financed by project bonds. this will help to maintain the union's competitiveness on the world market and to open up new employment opportunities for its citizens. it will have to be done, step by step, in the shortest possible time.

in writing. - i voted in favour of mrs berès' report because i agree with the content of the report on the policies to be adopted to promote employment in the eu. the new integrated guidelines of the europe 2020 strategy should be fully reflected in the policy measures and initiatives of the member states. the commitment of each member state to maintain the targets to be achieved by 2014 will be crucial. unemployment, especially youth unemployment, remains one of the objectives which requires the greatest effort to tackle it at its root, because it reduces not only the immediate spending capacity but also all future investment strategies, causing very serious social disadvantages which go beyond purely economic factors. not only the quantity of jobs, but also their quality must be increased, and this is a matter for the member states in particular, who must also continue their efforts to combat poverty and support social inclusion.
in writing. the food price index on financial markets shows that prices have risen uncontrollably in recent months, due to the international economic and financial crisis and also to the recent ecological disasters caused by climate change. but what makes this situation even worse is the speculative behaviour which has contributed up to 50% to the rise in prices, preventing many people from enjoying food security and generating, especially in the poorer countries, political instability, which, as we know, will eventually threaten the peace and security of other countries. food security is a fundamental human right, which is reiterated in the millennium development goals, as well as in the cap. the european union is therefore obliged to affirm its commitment to the creation of a sound policy of agricultural and rural development, its support for research and technological innovation in order to improve productivity, in compliance with the criteria of energy efficiency and sustainability. sustainability also means promoting the production and marketing of traditional local food products, offering appropriate financial incentives and the possibility of access to credit for smes. i also think it is important to adopt clear and transparent regulations, to prevent speculation, especially at the expense of the health of many european citizens, and to make european agricultural production competitive.
in writing. − climate change and speculation in commodity markets are among the main factors threatening food security, both inside and outside the eu. it is with this conviction that i support the resolution calling for urgent measures to combat the manipulation of food prices and to ensure that agricultural production is maintained in the eu. there is no doubt that droughts, floods, fires and storms - occurring more frequently than in the past - are reducing agricultural production capacity around the world. proper soil and water management is therefore essential to prevent the loss of arable land. it is also necessary to combat abusive speculation on the markets for foodstuffs, agricultural raw materials and energy. food security requires a strong policy that secures a future for our farmers and encourages the introduction of more effective and sustainable farming practices in the least developed countries.
in writing. − rising food prices are also causing difficulties for the eu. the steady increase over the past few months has reached figures never recorded before by fao. this is due to a whole host of factors, the lack of a global trade agreement, the rise in the prices of certain raw materials and the increased demand for food, but also to speculation and 'financial games' carried out on other markets but which have repercussions on the global market. in addition, there is the contrast between developed and developing economies, where the latter, hard but indirectly affected by the crisis, use food as the only weapon at their disposal. this situation has not only affected the global market but also small producers and consumers who are faced with increases, even large increases, in basic necessities. i therefore believe that food security is a priority which must be defended and pursued and that it is necessary and proper to seek a solution to this instability which is as comprehensive as possible and which is shared by all.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution because it strongly condemns the increase in the food price index, which in recent months has reached the highest level in 20 years, causing social emergencies such as the riots which have been rocking the whole of the maghreb since december. the increase in the cost of food is causing a sharp decline in the standard of living for the masses of workers, for whom food expenditure normally constitutes 50% of the household budget. in the european union alone, some 80 million people still live below the poverty line, many of them assisted by food aid programmes. the poor harvests in america, the natural disasters in russia and brazil, the rise in energy and oil prices, the ageing of the agricultural sector - these are the problems that must be tackled without further delay. it is more important than ever to condemn speculation and to study the possibility of a european food storage system to cope with crises such as the one we are experiencing. the aim is to seek shared collective strategies to respond promptly to the increase in demand for food, including through specific incentive policies that bring young people closer to the agricultural world.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this proposal for a regulation is intended to incorporate some of the recommendations adopted by the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean (gfcm) in order to help improve legal certainty and at the same time to be an important step towards simplification. to date, the recommendations adopted by the gfcm have been transposed into community legislation on a provisional basis, through annual regulations on fishing opportunities. the permanent nature of this recommendation, however, requires a more stable legal instrument for their transposition into community law. therefore, those recommendations should be transposed by a single legislative act to which future recommendations may be added by amending that legislative act. as regards the content of the recommendations adopted by the gfcm, title ii (technical measures) of the proposed regulation lays down certain restrictions on fishing within the gulf of lion as regards the fishing nets that can be used (article 5), the granting of licences for viable fishing activities and the protection of natural habitats. in addition, vessels authorised to participate in the fishing for lamprey are issued with a special fishing permit and included in a list provided to the commission by the member state (article 13). as regards fishing gear, the proposal for a regulation details the minimum mesh size of nets in the mediterranean (article 15) and the black sea (article 16) and prohibits the use of towed dredges and trawls at a depth of more than 1000 metres (article 17). title iii was entitled 'control measures'. among these is that each member state is required to send the european commission, via the usual computer support, an updated list of vessels of more than 15 metres in overall length, flying its flag and registered in its territory, authorised to fish in the gfcm area (article 18). the second chapter deals with measures concerning the port state. the scope of application covers third country vessels which may be subject to controls and inspections for landing and transhipment operations (article 21). in addition, member states shall not allow a third country vessel to use their ports if the vessel does not fly the flag of a cfp contracting party, if the vessel has engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing activities or if the vessel does not have a valid fishing authorisation (article 23). title iv (cooperation, information and reporting) of the proposed regulation provides for cooperation and exchange of information between the european commission and the member states and the executive secretary of the gfcm (article 24) and for the member states to transmit to the executive secretary of the gfcm statistical data (ship registration number, capacity, tonnage, horsepower, etc.) within the prescribed time limits. as regards the provisions of title v (final provisions), in particular article 28, it allows the commission, with the consent of the european parliament and of the council, to amend, by means of delegated acts, provisions which are not essential to the legislative act in question, in accordance with article 290 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. furthermore, it is noted that the cgpm contracting parties have an obligation to ensure full implementation of the agreed measures as from the date set by the cgpm itself. timely transposition is therefore necessary in order to make such international measures directly applicable to natural or legal persons at community level and to ensure legal certainty in that respect. however, the co-decision procedure, because of its length, seems to be over-stretched in this particular case with regard to the issues at stake in the transposition of the amendments to the provisions of article 28, which i consider to be non-essential and which, before being proposed or adopted at the annual session of the gfcm, have already been discussed and agreed with the member states, both in working groups in the council and on the spot at the same session. the fact that the european union is unable to ensure this transposition of community law within the time limit may be considered a breach of its international commitments. this, in turn, could undermine the credibility of the european union in the context of the gfcm and other international fisheries management organisations. this is not a good service to the european union and would certainly provide further evidence to the union's detractors, who might suspect that the european union is wasting time on small things instead of concentrating on the more substantial issues. finally, it is crucial to note that important safeguard mechanisms are built into the system of delegated acts, such as the possibility for the two co-legislators, the parliament and the council, to object to specific acts adopted by the commission on the basis of the delegated powers and the possibility to revoke the delegation entirely if they are not satisfied with the way in which these powers are used by the commission. i therefore think that article 28 on delegated acts is a good compromise which will be discussed with the council at second reading in order to reach a final agreement. this reasoning is in line with the report by ms bairbre de brún on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 998/2003 on the animal health requirements applicable to non-commercial movements of pet animals and the report by mr romeva on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a catch documentation programme for bluefin tuna.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i think that this measure will bring the mediterranean issues to an even more urgent stage than the acts we have already carried out. i believe that the act we are now adopting is much more important than the effects of the 2006 community regulation. i think this also meets some of the limitations of that regulation which, being unilateral, has left large fisheries sectors often supporting the idea that yes, europe is doing its part, but the other coastal countries are not. i think it is strategic for us to tackle the issue at this scale and with these characteristics. the work done by mr rivellini, which has been very well received, deserves, i think, a formal thank you from this house. however, i have the distinct feeling that the fact that we are unable to resolve this question at first reading and will come to a second reading, especially on the interpretation of article 28 of this regulation, raises a question: the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. parliament is basically saying that it is good that these delegated acts are in the hands of the commission and there is some resistance from the council, by the way, the absence today is also a significant absence. this act has given parliament a strong feeling that preserving biodiversity and maintaining the fish stocks of this important sea is also the future of fishermen. that said, i think that the stage we are now entering must be one in which the idea of codecision is again at the centre. these delegated acts have their own reason for being delegated and therefore conferred on the commission today, but international agreements must maintain its role in parliament when they do take place.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i share the rapporteur's view that the fisheries regulation should be simplified by means of a regulation which would incorporate the recommendations adopted by the committee on fisheries in the mediterranean. i share the objectives and principles of the common fisheries policy, but i believe that a fair balance must be struck in all coastal member states between socioeconomic value and the protection of ecosystems. i believe that the special interests of local communities must also be protected. this regulation lays down the details of the gear permitted for fishing in the waters of the gfcm area, in particular the mediterranean. i would point out that the objective of safeguarding our natural habitats has serious implications for some fishing communities. italy is awaiting a derogation from the commission's de facto ban on fishing for two particular species which are the main product of a large marine industry. in conclusion, i would like to call on all the representatives of the 27 member states and the commission to consider whether it would be appropriate to make these instruments less rigid in the face of the survival needs of a local fisheries sector.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i think we have two problems, one of method and the other of substance in this matter. the method is that we are using a device - and we thank mr fraga for it - that of the oral question, to talk about something which should, after the treaty of lisbon, be a right of this parliament. i think that this practice must be stopped. we cannot use a strategy to accompany a codecision process. the co-decision is such when it is cultivated in the stages in which it matures. today we have this debate, it ends, the treaty goes ahead and we say yes or no at the end. this method needs to be converted. on the substance, however, i only wanted to emphasize, and i agree with many of my colleagues, the measurement of the effects of fisheries agreements, because these are not just trade agreements through which we go to mauritania to buy cephalopods at 1 euro per kilo. they need to be able to measure both sustainability and, above all, the impact on the economy of that country, to understand how many jobs are changing, to understand what the rate of innovation is for artisanal fishing, to understand the use of these resources. it is not just a simple trade deal, but a fisheries agreement with all its implications.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i congratulate my colleague, mrs schaldemose, on the constructive and fruitful cooperation we have had. the point i would like to make here is the one i introduced in the itre committee's opinion, which mr schaldemose - and i thank you again - shared and took up in his report, namely the request to the european commission to consider the use of new technologies and materials, such as the use of microchips or radio frequencies, to enable better product identification, thus respecting consumer safety and at optimized costs. this would provide complete traceability, since the consumer would be able to know all the aspects of the product, including the various stages of processing, the origin of the materials and the identity of the responsible parties. it would also eliminate the problem of identifying a criterion for the attribution of the origin and the 'made in' of a product. in fact, it is for this very reason that we have seen that to call a product 'made in france' when only the last stage of processing has taken place in this country is a way of deceiving the consumer. i therefore strongly urge the commissioner to act on this request from the european parliament, which is certainly speaking on behalf of the citizens and consumers of europe.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, to date the recommendations adopted by the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean have been transposed into community legislation on a provisional basis by means of annual regulations on fishing opportunities. these concern conservation, management, exploitation, control and marketing measures for fishery and aquaculture products in the mediterranean. the permanent nature of these recommendations, however, requires a more stable legal instrument for their transposition into community law. it is therefore appropriate to transpose those recommendations by means of a single legislative act to which future recommendations may be added. we have done that today and this will improve legal certainty and at the same time be an important step towards simplification. at this point, the gfcm contracting parties have an obligation to ensure full implementation of the agreed measures as from the date set and timely transposition was therefore necessary in order to make those international measures directly applicable to natural or legal persons at community level and to ensure legal certainty in this respect.

in writing. - we support the own-initiative report, as we all realise that the excessive alarmism linked to the alleged avian influenza pandemic has cost the eu about 10 times more than the normal influenza campaign. accepting the who's warning without acting independently through cost and risk analyses carried out by the european agencies ecdc and ema has led to costly and unnecessary vaccination campaigns and in particular to pushing the population to buy disproportionate quantities of disposable sterile material and disinfectants. in the end the result in terms of deaths, which is what the legislator should be most concerned about, was even lower than that of a normal seasonal influence. it is therefore essential that the commission informs parliament within six months of a detailed cost-benefit analysis and of how it intends to deal with similar situations in the future. the who should revise the definition of pandemic to take account of both the geographical extent and the severity of the infection.
